what_it_does: Running a large language model (an AI text system like Gemma-2B) directly on a smartphone is desirable for privacy and offline use, but doing so is far too slow for real-time tasks such as understanding what is on the screen. Modern smartphones contain a dedicated AI accelerator chip called an NPU (Neural Processing Unit) — a fixed-function unit optimized for the regular matrix math that dominates neural network inference — but LLMs have an irregular, attention-heavy structure (the mechanism by which the model relates every word to every other word) that does not map cleanly onto what NPUs expect. This work identifies the specific mismatches, then redesigns the inference pipeline by fusing multiple small operations into single larger NPU-friendly operations, partitioning the work into chunks that fit the NPU's fixed memory, and overlapping NPU computation with CPU work so neither sits idle. The focus is on the 'prefill' phase — where the model ingests the whole input prompt at once — because that is the dominant bottleneck for interactive response time.
